title: Pauri 22, meaning: worlds beyond worlds
hook: underworlds beyond underworlds, skies beyond skies; if it could be written it would be, but the writing runs out (Japji 22)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 22. Your line was paataalaa paataal: underworlds below underworlds, skies beyond skies. Today, what happens to anyone who tries to measure them. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

Every notebook has a last page. Somebody sets out to list everything visible from a hilltop: each roof, each tree, each bird. The first notebook fills. Then a shelf of them. The handwriting gets shaky, and the view hasn't gotten any smaller. At some point, the one writing runs out before the view does. Pauri 22 says something like that, and it isn't sad about it. It's almost relieved. It says: this was never going to fit on paper.
screen: `LISTING EVERYTHING IN VIEW.` → `A NOTEBOOK, THEN A SHELF.` → `THE WRITER RUNS OUT FIRST.`

segments.voice: After underworlds below underworlds and skies beyond skies, Pauri 22 goes on, in paraphrase. People searched and searched for the farthest edge, and grew tired. The Vedas say this one thing: there's no end to find. The books of the Semitic traditions, the Kateb, speak of eighteen thousand worlds; but at the root there is one source. Notice what Guru Nanak does there. He gathers the scriptures of the two communities around him, Hindu and Muslim, and hears them both pointing the same direction: past counting, toward one. He doesn't set them against each other. Then the line behind today's carry. If there were an account, the stanza says, you could write it down. But the account perishes in the writing. In the original: lekhaa hoe ta likheeai lekhai hoe vinaas. Lekhaa is an account, a ledger, a tally. Vinaas is destruction, perishing. Commentators read it two ways. The account itself falls apart before it's done. Or the one writing it perishes before the account is finished. Either way: the writing runs out. And the stanza ends, in paraphrase: Nanak says, call Him great; He alone knows Himself. That's not giving up. It's the same move Japji has been making since Pauri 12: no pen for this. It's the right size of a human being, standing under the sky. We can say great. We can't write the whole ledger. The ledger stays unfinished, and the sky is still there to look at.
screen: `THEY SEARCHED, AND GREW TIRED.` · `THE VEDAS, THE KATEB, ONE SOURCE.` · `LEKHAA HOE TA LIKHEEAI.` · `CALL HIM GREAT; HE KNOWS HIMSELF.` · then, large: `THE WRITING RUNS OUT.`

segments.voice: If you can, look at the sky for a minute: through a window, from a doorway, or step outside. If you can't see it, close your eyes and picture the widest sky you remember. Don't try to name or count what's there. Just look, and let it be bigger than you. When the minute is up, close your eyes and sit with the size of it. The bell holds the time.
Lekhaa, an account or ledger. Worlds beyond worlds; the searchers grow tired; if it could be written, it would be, but the writing runs out. Call Him great.
Your line: the writing runs out. Today, when a list or a worry keeps growing, stop writing it for a moment and look up. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Pauri 22 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; Sikhs often cite its closing, that only the One knows Himself, when speaking of the limits of human description.

fork.setup: you set out to write the full account of every world. what does Pauri 22 say happens?
options: you finish it with enough notebooks.
the writing runs out before the worlds do.
you find the last world at the edge.
fork.reveal: if there were an account, it would be written; but the account perishes in the writing. Nanak says: call Him great.

original.note: Gurmukhi: lekhaa, an account or ledger; in Pauri 22, the account that perishes in the writing.

trapdoor: what you thought: creation is very big.
what it means: creation is past every search and every ledger; the fitting word is great, and the One alone knows.
what a scholar hears: sahas athaarah, eighteen thousand worlds, echoes a number known in Islamic tradition; lekhai hoe vinaas is read as the account perishing, or the writer perishing first.

notes: Line 2 (ved kahan ik vaat) is read variously: the Vedas say one thing, or the Vedas say with one voice (there is no end). Paraphrased as 'the Vedas say this one thing: there's no end to find'; confirm.
Kateb glossed as the books of the Semitic traditions; the eighteen thousand worlds is a figure found in Islamic tradition. Confirm.
'Asuloo ik dhaat' paraphrased as 'at the root there is one source'; confirm.
Two readings of lekhai hoe vinaas offered; confirm.
